A city in an empire that forgot it was still an empire

By 2030, the United States has spent decades looking inward. The federal government is diminished; states and municipalities shoulder more of their own crises. Globally, Brussels, Beijing, and New Delhi set the pace. In Port Carrick, old industrial losses, public distrust, and a three-way mayoral race make national decline feel local.

This is a worldbuilding reference, not a systems guide. It distinguishes project-established details, author-established alternate history, and proposed archive material.

01 / The setting

The enemy within

Retro-contemporary America, 2030: familiar institutions, unfamiliar weight.

United States · author canon

Still united. Less federal.

The United States remains the United States, but it is no longer the global superpower. The federal government has lost much of its domestic reach. States and municipalities exercise substantially more autonomy, and must face more crises without reliable federal assistance.

Governors have become regional kings; mayors, elected lords. The language is half-joke, half-description: local governments hold more responsibility because fewer institutions above them can or will step in. The country is a declining continental empire people sometimes forget still technically exists.

Daily mood · author canon

Distrust as ambient normal

There is little public attention left for distant adversaries. Political coalitions point fingers at each other and argue over who hollowed out the country. Ethnic enclaves increasingly sequester themselves in more homogeneous neighborhoods; suspicion crosses city blocks and institutions.

This is a social pressure, not a universal personality. Port Carrick still has neighbors, institutions, friendships, and civic loyalties that cut across those lines.

02 / The world before Port Carrick

Alternate-history timeline

Turning points are author canon. Exact dates and many intervening events remain open.

  1. 1960s
    No one reaches the Moon

    No crewed lunar landing occurs. The failure turns the space race into a lasting cultural disappointment and makes the public more cynical about national promises and grand projects.

  2. 1960s →
    Martin Luther King Jr. is never assassinated

    King lives to old age and dies naturally. Without his martyrdom, the civil-rights movement does not consolidate around one defining loss. Younger activists take up leadership, and the struggle lasts longer.

  3. 1960s–2000s
    Vietnam becomes a generational wound

    The Vietnam War continues into the early 2000s. Washington calls its final departure a “dignified withdrawal”; the U.S.-supported government collapses almost immediately. The episode permanently wounds the American public spirit.

  4. Late 20th c.
    The Soviet Union contracts, rather than collapsing

    The Union shrinks considerably, becomes more federal and somewhat modernized, and grows much more religious. It adopts the name Christian Confederation of the Nations of the Caucuses (CCNC). It survives as a changed and diminished power.

  5. 2000s–2030
    The center of gravity moves

    The European Union, China, and India become the dominant forces on the global stage. The United States and the CCNC are often disregarded as self-interested “lions in winter.” America turns inward and its global relevance wanes for decades.

  6. 2030
    Local power carries the weight

    With limited federal support, states and municipalities exercise more autonomy and face more direct exposure when a crisis arrives. In Port Carrick, the city’s industrial decline and strained public finances sit behind a three-way mayoral election.

Dates are intentionally broad. The historical newspaper covers below provide illustrative issue dates and headlines; except for the broad turning points in this timeline, those specific dates and reported events are not locked canon.
03 / Local history

Port Carrick, Great Lakes

A fictional port city whose old employment base disappeared without a replacement.

Industry and decline · project lore

Steel, parts, and the missing next chapter

Port Carrick grew around its harbor, steel mill, and parts plants. The steel mill and parts plants were lost; the city never replaced them with an economic base of comparable scale. Port Carrick remains financially strained and short on confidence about what comes next.

The exact dates of the closures, the companies involved, and the civic choices that followed are not set. The city’s industrial loss is established; a detailed chronology is still open.

City premiseExact dates open
The city in 2030 · project lore

Election year, inherited scandal

The player character is the new chief of the Port Carrick Police Department, appointed by Mayor Dale Pruett. The former chief resigned over a scandal; the city is left with the consequences and open questions. Port Carrick is nearing a three-way mayoral election as its finances worsen.

The identity of the former chief and the details of the scandal have not been established.

Campaign settingScandal details open

04 / Character files

The people around City Hall

The candidates are fictional. Their formal party affiliations are not yet named.

Mayor · incumbent

Dale Pruett

“Pruett: It Mostly Works.”

A competent, aggressively boring administrator with few reform ideas. His stump-speech world is procurement timelines and municipal process. In a city on the edge of failure, Pruett’s refusal to sound dramatic can read as either steadiness or denial.

Project loreAdministrator
Council President

Victor Garrow

A corrupt authoritarian who is openly pro-police and has the union’s ear. He holds the city’s towing and demolition contracts, and argues for curfews and emergency powers. He represents a vision of Port Carrick where order is bought, granted, and enforced from above.

Project loreContractsEmergency powers
Councillor

Anne Halvorsen

A democratic socialist who genuinely wants to help the city and is sharply critical of the police. She speaks from a tradition of tenant and community organizing. Her exact personal history, relationships, and constituency beyond that broad description remain open.

Project loreTenant organizingAccountability
The player character · new chief

A blank slate by design

The chief’s name, gender, appearance, and age are chosen by the player. No fixed biography or demographic profile defines the character. Ethnicity and religion can subtly shape a few factional affinities or create friction where none otherwise existed, but these influences are minor and do not dictate a person’s loyalties.

Author canonPersonal history open
Former police chief · identity unknown

The vacant office

The previous chief resigned over a scandal before the player character’s appointment. The departure is part of Port Carrick’s present civic distrust, but the former chief’s name, motives, and exact wrongdoing are not established.

06 / Political field

Three candidates, party names still open

Local power is personal and municipal. No candidate is tied to a real-world party.

The 2030 mayoral contest

Three visions for a city running out of room

The project establishes three fictional candidates, but does not specify registered party names or whether they run on formal party tickets. These descriptions are political blocs, not official party brands.

The shorthand names are editorial placeholders only. They should not be repeated as canon party names unless the project adopts them.

United States · party system

National labels not yet defined

The alternate United States is politically consumed by domestic blame and uneven local crises. The names, structure, and platforms of its national parties have not been established. Port Carrick’s candidates should not be mapped one-to-one onto contemporary real parties.

Federalism · author canon

Local offices with lordly reach

Governors and mayors possess more practical authority as federal capacity recedes. Port Carrick’s mayoral office is consequential because the city must solve local problems with limited help from Washington—not because its mayor commands a healthy, well-funded machine.
